summary: The product of a design team in the Traffic Engineering Working Group that collected requirements for network hierarchy and survivability in service provider networks. It adds expanded definitions and suggests a small set of interoperable survivability approaches.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3386 collects what service providers need from a network that has to keep working when something fails. It defines the terms first, then lists four recovery mechanisms with a target time for each, and explains how the layers of a network should take turns recovering instead of colliding with one another.

questions: how do network layers recover from failures
what is the difference between protection and restoration
what is a shared risk group
what is a hold off timer in multilayer recovery
subtitle: What service providers need from a network that must keep working after a failure

tldr.problem: Service providers needed a shared vocabulary and a small set of interoperable ways to survive link, span and equipment failures, and a way for the different layers and areas of a network to recover without fighting each other.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines protection, restoration and recovery, compares the trade-offs, and requires four mechanisms: 1:1 path protection with pre-established capacity, 1:1 path protection with pre-planned capacity, local restoration, and path restoration, each with a target recovery time.
tldr.outcome: It sets out requirements rather than a protocol, and gives later Traffic Engineering and CCAMP work a common set of terms and timing bounds to aim at. Coordination between layers is left to nested hold-off timers rather than signalling between layers.

today: RFC 3386 is an Informational memo published in November 2002, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a requirements and definitions document: its purpose was to focus the work of the Traffic Engineering and CCAMP working groups, and it defines no protocol of its own.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
RFC 3386 is the result of a design team in the Traffic Engineering Working Group that collected current and near-term requirements for survivability and hierarchy in service provider networks. It is a requirements document with an expanded set of definitions attached, so that later proposals have shared terms to work with.

The team found a need for a small set of interoperable survivability approaches in packet and non-packet networks, operating primarily at a single network layer. On hierarchy, it found no driving near-term need for vertical hierarchy, meaning direct exchange of signalling and routing between layers such as TDM or optical and MPLS. What was needed instead was looser coordination, such as the specification of hold-off timers. For horizontal hierarchy, within one network layer, there are several pressing needs, chief among them the ability to set up many Label Switched Paths in a service provider network with a hierarchical Interior Gateway Protocol, which is needed to support layer 2 and layer 3 Virtual Private Network services that require edge-to-edge signalling across a core network.

The initial focus is intra-domain operations. Rules governing survivability mechanisms at domain boundaries must also be specified to keep end-to-end service consistent in a multi-provider environment, though the document does not treat those issues in depth.
sections.plainLanguage: This document collects what service providers need from a network that must keep working when something fails. It defines the terms first, then lists a small set of recovery mechanisms, the time each should take, and the rules for the layers of a network to work together.

sections.title: Survivability Terms
sections.content:
Survivability is the capability of a network to maintain service continuity in the presence of faults within the network. Mechanisms are implemented on a per-link basis, a per-path basis, or throughout an entire network, and the degree of survivability is determined by the network's capability to survive single failures, multiple failures and equipment failures.

A working entity is what carries traffic in normal operation: a channel or transmission link in the physical layer, a Label Switched Path in MPLS, or a logical bundle of one or more of those. A protection entity, also called a backup or recovery entity, carries the protected traffic in recovery operation, when the working entity is in error or has failed. Extra traffic, also called preemptable traffic, is traffic carried over the protection entity while the working entity is active; it is not protected, and it is preempted when the protection entity is needed for the real traffic.

A shared risk group is a set of network elements collectively impacted by a specific fault or fault type. A shared risk link group is the union of all the links on those fibres that are routed in the same physical conduit. The document notes that these groups are sensitive information, because an adversary who knows which elements share a risk can design an attack and judge its scope.

Recovery is the sequence of events and actions after a failure is detected, to maintain the required performance level for existing services. It has two parallel parts: a repair process with fault isolation and repair of the failed components, and a reconfiguration process using survivability mechanisms. In protection, reconfiguration means switching the affected traffic from a working entity to a protection entity. In restoration, it means path selection and rerouting. Normalization is the sequence of actions that returns the network to its preferred state once the repair is complete, and revertive mode means the traffic is automatically switched back to the repaired working entity, while non-revertive mode means it is not.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sorts out the words first. A working entity carries traffic normally, a protection entity takes over when it fails, and restoration means finding a different route after a failure instead of having one ready in advance.

sections.title: Protection Compared with Restoration
sections.content:
Protection, also called protection switching, is based on predetermined failure recovery: as the working entity is established, a protection entity is established too. Four architectures are named, 1+1, 1:1, 1:n and m:n. In 1+1 the protection entity is dedicated to each working entity and the working entity is permanently bridged onto it, so identical traffic is transmitted on both and the receiving end selects one according to predetermined criteria. In 1:1 the protection entity is also dedicated, but the traffic normally runs only on the working entity, and both ends of the protected domain must signal detection of the fault and initiate the switchover. In 1:n one protection entity is shared by n working entities, so not all of the affected traffic may be protected. The m:n architecture generalises that, with m dedicated protection entities shared by n working entities, and has rarely been implemented or standardized.

Restoration, also called recovery by rerouting, establishes new paths or path segments on demand, using resources that are currently unassigned in the same layer. Preemption of extra traffic may be used if no spare resources are available. The choice of a recovery path may be based on preplanned configurations, network routing policies, or the current state of the network, and signalling is used to establish the new paths that bypass the fault.

The trade-off is the point of the comparison. Protection techniques usually offer fast recovery from failure with enhanced availability, because the backup is already there. Restoration techniques usually achieve better resource utilisation, because nothing is committed until the fault occurs and its location is known, but they are inherently slower and their time varies with the amount of traffic to restore, the topology and the severity of the fault. The 1+1 architecture is rather expensive, since resource duplication is required, and is generally used for services that need very high availability. A 1:1 architecture is inherently slower than 1+1, because both ends of the protection domain must communicate to perform the switchover, but its protection path can optionally carry low-priority extra traffic in normal operation if preemption is allowed. Packet networks can pre-establish a protection path with pre-planned but not pre-reserved capacity, so no bandwidth is consumed while no packets are sent, which is not the case in transmission networks such as optical or TDM, where path establishment and resource reservation cannot be decoupled.
sections.plainLanguage: Protection keeps a spare path ready and switches to it, which is fast but costs capacity. Restoration finds a new route after the failure, which is slower but uses the network better. The document asks operators to choose between them per service.

sections.title: The Required Set of Mechanisms
sections.content:
The initial scope is backhoe failures in the inter-office connections of a service provider network, which show up as link and span failures. Systematic control-plane failure, configuration error, breaches of security and congestion that reduces throughput are out of scope.

Four mechanisms are required.

  • 1:1 path protection with pre-established capacity. The head end of a working connection establishes a protection connection to the destination. Traffic is only sent on the working connection in normal operation, and the capacity in the protection connection is pre-established, though in non-packet networks it should be able to carry preemptable extra traffic. Head ends need to create connections that are as failure-disjoint as possible, which requires shared risk group information that can be assigned to either nodes or links and propagated through the control or management plane.
  • 1:1 path protection with pre-planned capacity. The protection connection is still pre-signalled, but the capacity may be shared, or double-booked. The operator provisions different amounts of protection capacity according to expected failure modes and service level agreements, and restoration capacity on each link can be shared by shared-risk-group-disjoint failures. If capacity is planned but not allocated, some form of signalling may be needed before traffic can be sent on protection connections, especially in TDM networks. The approach improves network resource utilisation but may require more careful planning.
  • Local restoration. Because of the time impact of signal propagation, dynamic recovery of an entire path may not meet the service requirements of some networks, so the connectivity of the link or span in immediate proximity to the fault is restored instead. Head end systems must have some control over whether their connections are candidates for local restoration. Best-effort and preemptable traffic may be excluded, and it is restored only if bandwidth is available.
  • Path restoration. Connections that are impacted by a fault are rerouted by the originating network element when it is notified of the connection failure. This source-based approach is efficient for network resources but typically takes longer, and it involves no new mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Four recovery methods are required: two kinds of reserved backup path, repairing the link right next to the break, and rerouting the whole connection from its starting point.

sections.title: Timing Bounds for Recovery
sections.content:
The bounds were chosen to cover a spectrum of mechanisms, and the document says plainly that none of the team would likely attest to the scientific merit of these bounds for any specific application. Two assumptions are made: approaches in which protection switches without propagation of information are likely to be faster than those that require some form of fault notification to some or all elements, and approaches that require signalling after a fault also suffer some timing impact. All the bounds exclude signal propagation.

  • 1:1 path protection with pre-established capacity: 100-500 ms
  • 1:1 path protection with pre-planned capacity: 100-750 ms
  • Local restoration: 50 ms
  • Path restoration: 1-5 seconds

The applications behind those numbers differ. Best-effort data only needs network connectivity recovered by rerouting at the IP layer. Premium data services need to meet TCP timeout or application protocol timer requirements. Voice is the tightest case, because call cutoff is in the range of 140 msec to 2 sec, the time a person waits after the speech path is interrupted before hanging up, or the time a telephone switch disconnects a call. Other real-time services such as streaming and fax terminate the session if the interruption is too long, and mission-critical applications such as real-time financial transactions cannot tolerate even brief interruptions.

Restoration priority must be implemented so that the order in which connections are restored matches the service requirements, and so that higher-priority traffic gets access to the best paths first. Preemption priority is used only when not all connections can be restored, and then the connections with the lower preemption priority are released.
sections.plainLanguage: Each recovery method has a target time, from 50 milliseconds for a local repair to one to five seconds for rerouting a whole connection. Voice is why the fast ones matter: a person gives up on a call after roughly 140 milliseconds to two seconds of silence.

sections.title: Coordinating Layers and Hierarchies
sections.content:
When a network has several technology layers, recovery has to be coordinated between them. The default mechanism is nested timers and the fault monitoring that SDH/SONET already provides. If lower-layer recovery happens over a longer period than higher-layer recovery, a hold-off timer avoids contention between the single-layer schemes, so each higher multiplexing level operates on a protection or restoration time scale greater than the layer below it. Where SDH/SONET protection switching is used, MPLS recovery timers must wait until SDH/SONET has had time to switch. Setting those timers trades rapid recovery against a race in which several layers respond to the same fault and allocate resources inefficiently. Where the lower layer has no restoration capability or is not expected to protect, for example an unprotected SDH/SONET linear circuit, there must be a mechanism for the lower layer to indicate immediately to the higher layer that a fault has occurred. Faults at higher layers should not trigger restoration or protection actions at lower layers.

On hierarchy, the document says effort should go to mechanisms that allow more scalable edge-to-edge signalling, rather than to mechanisms that interconnect networks at different layers. A large network is partitioned into smaller non-overlapping sub-networks by topology, function, administrative policy or service domain, and routing information is aggregated at the boundaries. Examples of horizontal hierarchy are BGP confederations, separate Autonomous Systems, and multi-area OSPF. The main driver for intra-domain horizontal hierarchy is edge-to-edge signalling for layer 2 and layer 3 VPNs, and the number of tunnels needed for VPNs is expected to stay within the scalability bounds of current protocols and implementations.

Where a connection crosses a hierarchical boundary, the document suggests concatenating survivability schemes: each part of the connection is protected within its own area, and the boundary is handled either by a device that takes part on both sides, such as an OSPF area border router, or by a least common denominator mechanism such as 1+1 port protection. A standardized means is also needed for the scheme on one side of the boundary to tell the scheme on the other side whether its recovery succeeded, so that a side whose part of the connection is already down does not recover again.
sections.plainLanguage: When several layers can recover on their own, the higher one waits for the lower one using timers, so they do not both react to the same fault and waste capacity. Across area boundaries, each part of a connection is protected inside its own area and the parts are joined together.

viz.caption: THE FOUR REQUIRED MECHANISMS AND THEIR TIMING BOUNDS

items.title: 1:1 with pre-established capacity
items.text: A protection path is set up with its capacity before the fault. Bound: 100-500 ms.

items.title: 1:1 with pre-planned capacity
items.text: A protection path is set up and the capacity is shared or double-booked. Bound: 100-750 ms.

items.title: Local restoration
items.text: The link or span next to the fault is repaired in place. Bound: 50 ms.

items.title: Path restoration
items.text: The originating element reroutes the connection after the failure notification. Bound: 1-5 seconds.

viz.caption: LAYERS THAT CARRY THEIR OWN SURVIVABILITY MECHANISMS

layers.label: IP
layers.detail: Rerouting restores service continuity after link and node outages, once routing has converged.

layers.label: MPLS
layers.detail: Work is under way to provide restoration here; recovery timers wait for the layer below.

layers.label: SDH/SONET
layers.detail: Automatic protection switching, plus self-healing ring and mesh restoration.

layers.label: Optical
layers.detail: Dynamic ring and mesh restoration, in addition to traditional 1+1 or 1:1 protection.
